sections.h2: Steps to sell a house in Plum Borough
sections.html:
Plum requires a Residential Occupancy Permit whenever the occupancy of a home changes, which includes a sale. The owner files a Residential Occupancy Transfer Application with the Community Development office, pays $100 and then schedules an inspection. Once the house passes, the borough issues the permit.

Timing is the part to plan. The application has to be signed by the owner and submitted at least five business days before the inspection date you request. After it arrives, a building inspector contacts you to set a day and time. The borough posts a list of what inspectors look for, so read it and fix small items before the visit.

  • Fee: $100, payable by check to the Borough of Plum.
  • Lead time: five business days before the requested inspection.
  • Limit: the borough requires the permit for a change in ownership or residents, but no more than once every two years regardless of how many changes occur.
  • Result: a passing inspection produces the Occupancy Permit.

sections.h2: Transfer tax for a Plum seller
sections.html:
Selling in Plum triggers a 2% realty transfer tax. The borough gets half a percent, the Plum School District gets half a percent and the Commonwealth gets 1%. You write a separate check for it when Allegheny County records the deed, apart from the recording fees.

Your sales agreement settles who pays. Close relatives transferring a house may only have to add a sentence to the deed naming the relationship; other exemptions go through the state's Statement of Value.

Northeast of Pittsburgh, with the Allegheny River along its northern side, Plum borders Monroeville, Penn Hills, Oakmont and, across the river, Cheswick, Springdale and Lower Burrell. It covers 28.57 square miles of land, which makes it the state's second-largest borough by area. Postal mail may carry a Pittsburgh address, even though the borough is outside the city limits.

The estimate for July 2025 is 26,225 residents, about 3.4% below the 2020 base of 27,147. The 2020 census counted 11,869 housing units, 4.7% of them vacant.

  • Middle home value is $227,600 in the 2020 to 2024 estimates, and 80.7% of households own.
  • Median household income: $98,705.
  • Persons per household: 2.45, and 22.8% of residents are 65 or older.
  • Median gross rent: $1,177.

The Pennsylvania Turnpike crosses Plum between mile markers 49 and 55, and the Plum Borough School District serves the borough.

Unpermitted work tends to surface when a buyer or inspector looks around. Community Development issues residential building permits for new dwellings, additions, decks, porches and porch roofs, pools deeper than 24 inches, structural alterations and demolitions. Zoning certificates cover front yard fences, sheds, detached garages, carports, gazebos and similar structures under 200 square feet.

If you added a deck or shed yourself, ask Community Development whether a permit or certificate is on file before the inspection. Fixing a paperwork gap before the occupancy visit is simpler than doing it after a buyer raises the question. The department also administers subdivision, conditional use and variance requests, which matter if the lot is large enough to split.

Plum parcels carry values from the Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments, set to a 2012 base year, so treat them as something other than today's market price. To contest one, go to the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review during the yearly window, which runs from July 1 to early September.

Ask the county treasurer and the Plum tax collectors for a paid-to-date statement before closing. Any balance owed gets paid from the sale proceeds, and a title search will show open amounts. The county also runs a homestead exclusion under Act 50 for owner-occupied homes, and a buyer who will live in the house applies through the county.

sections.h2: What a Plum seller must disclose
sections.html:
Chapter 73 of Title 68 requires you to give the buyer a signed, dated property disclosure statement ahead of signing the agreement of transfer. The statement covers the roof, basement, structure, plumbing, electrical systems, heating and cooling, water and sewage service, land and drainage, hazardous substances and title issues. It also asks about the condition and location of storm water facilities and whether the owner or someone else maintains them.

The seller doesn't need to carry out special testing but may not say anything known to be false or leave out a known material defect. Delivery can be in person, by first class mail, by certified mail or by fax. A disclosure can be amended in writing before the agreement is signed.

  • Condominium sellers disclose only about their own unit.
  • Estate fiduciaries are outside the chapter.
  • A buyer's damages suit must begin within two years after final settlement.

Choose the route first, then line up the permit. A listing reaches the most buyers, a sale by owner saves the commission, and a cash sale tends to shorten the schedule. All three still need the Plum occupancy inspection before the deed transfers, so book it as soon as you have a target closing date.

  • Submit the occupancy application at least five business days ahead of the inspection date.
  • Check the borough's inspector checklist and fix small items beforehand.
  • Confirm permits for any deck, porch or shed you built.
  • Ask the settlement agent for the 2% transfer tax figure and the payoff before you accept terms.

With the permit issued, you sign the deed at the table. Recording follows, the transfer tax goes in on its own check, and the title company settles your loan and any open tax before handing you what is left. Paying cash removes the lender's appraisal and approval, so the schedule depends chiefly on the inspection and the title search.

A house sold within the past two years needs a call to Community Development about the permit limit, so the application doesn't stall. For a rental, put the tenant's move-out date in writing so the inspector walks an empty house. Before you set a date, collect the deed, your lender's payoff figure and any permit paperwork for decks, porches or sheds, and keep the $100 check ready so the application can go in the same day you decide to sell.

faqs.q: Does Plum Borough require an occupancy permit to sell a house?
faqs.a: Yes. A Residential Occupancy Permit is required when the occupancy of a home changes. The owner files the application with a $100 fee, an inspector schedules a visit, and a passing inspection gets the permit.

faqs.q: How far ahead must I apply for the Plum occupancy inspection?
faqs.a: Apply at least five business days before the inspection date you want. The owner signs the application, and the check is payable to the Borough of Plum. An inspector then contacts you to set the day and time.

faqs.q: How much is the transfer tax in Plum Borough?
faqs.a: It is 2% in total: 0.5% to the borough, 0.5% to the Plum School District and 1% to the state. Allegheny County collects it when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Can Plum require a new occupancy permit every time ownership changes?
faqs.a: Not more than once every two years. The borough caps the permit at one every two years regardless of how many changes happen. Ask Community Development how that rule applies if the home changed hands recently.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my Allegheny County assessment?
faqs.a: The annual window opens July 1 and closes in early September. Watch the county's real estate portal for the exact dates if you think your value is off.
